Kotlin Multiplatform, from the compiler up · check

Know Living on iOS already?

One question for each of the 6 puzzles in this module. A right answer marks that puzzle as passed, so you can jump ahead. A wrong one tells you which puzzle to start with. Nothing is sent anywhere: it's saved in this browser.

Puzzle 7: Counting or tracing

Two objects point only at each other; nothing else points at them. What does a tracing GC do?

Not quite. Neither is reachable, so both are freed. Learn it in puzzle 7 →

Not quite. Tracing doesn't count; it frees what it can't reach from the roots. Learn it in puzzle 7 →

Right. Unreachable means freed, cycles included.

Puzzle 8: Weak references and closures

The screen stores a closure that uses self strongly. The user leaves. What happens?

Not quite. Leaving doesn't change counts; the closure still holds the screen. Learn it in puzzle 8 →

Right. Self stores a closure that holds self: a cycle.

Not quite. The screen holds the closure, so neither count reaches zero. Learn it in puzzle 8 →

Puzzle 9: Two ways to free memory

Kotlin holds a Swift object, then lets go. When does Swift's deinit run?

Right. Release follows Kotlin's GC, not the moment of letting go.

Not quite. It's freed, only later: at the next garbage collection. Learn it in puzzle 9 →

Not quite. Kotlin's hold is released by the collector, so the Swift object waits for the next GC. Learn it in puzzle 9 →

Puzzle 10: The main thread on iOS

Which iOS piece plays the role of Android's MessageQueue?

Not quite. UIKit is the screen framework; tasks wait in the main queue. Learn it in puzzle 10 →

Not quite. The run loop is the Looper; the line of waiting tasks is the main queue. Learn it in puzzle 10 →

Right. The waiting line is the main queue.

Puzzle 11: Whose thread is it?

Your shared code resumes a coroutine on Dispatchers.Main on iOS. Which thread runs it?

Right. Main is still the main thread on iOS.

Not quite. The dispatcher decides, not the caller: Main means the main queue. Learn it in puzzle 11 →

Not quite. On iOS, Main is backed by the main queue, so it still runs on the main thread. Learn it in puzzle 11 →

Puzzle 12: One framework, not two

An app imports two Kotlin frameworks, and both contain the same User class. Swift passes a User from one to the other. What happens?

Not quite. Each framework has its own runtime and its own copy of the class; to Swift they're different types. Learn it in puzzle 12 →

Right. Two frameworks, two copies of every type.

Not quite. Where the class came from doesn't help: two frameworks, two types. Learn it in puzzle 12 →
